title: Our Mutual Friend: A Literary Discussion

segments.title: Inheritance and Imposture: The Novel's Central Mystery

utterances.text: Welcome to Our Mutual Friend Unpacked — a close, passionate, and occasionally heated look at one of the greatest novels in the English language.
I'm your host, and over this series we'll be working through Charles Dickens's last completed novel — a book that is by turns comic, grotesque, tender, and devastating.
Our Mutual Friend is a novel about money — who has it, who wants it, who it destroys — and about identity: who we pretend to be, and whether we can become someone better.
Today we're opening with the novel's central mystery: the inheritance, the imposture, and the question of who John Harmon really is.
Joining me are three extraordinary readers of this book, and I want to introduce them properly.
Dr. Eleanor Hartley is a novelist and creative writing teacher who is obsessed — in the best possible way — with how Dickens builds his effects from the inside out.
When Eleanor reads a novel, she sees the architecture — the load-bearing sentences, the structural choices that hold everything up.
Oliver Trevelyan has lent his voice to more classic audiobooks than perhaps anyone alive, and he comes to every novel as a performer first.
He hears the rhythms Dickens wrote for the voice — the comic timing, the grotesque relish — and he is an incomparable guide to that dimension of the text.
And Caroline Woodcourt is a book critic who first read Our Mutual Friend as a teenager and has returned to it many times since.

She reads for the experience — what moves you, what makes you laugh, what makes you stop and read a sentence again — and she has strong opinions about which characters deserve better from their author.
Let's begin at the beginning of the mystery — with the Boffins, and with what it means to inherit a fortune built on dust.
What strikes me immediately about how Dickens frames this inheritance is that it arrives already tainted — morally, emotionally, even physically.
The money is supposed to redeem old Harmon's sins against his son — and the very moment it might do that, the son is dead.
Boffin puts it with this wonderful blunt precision, speaking to Mortimer Lightwood.
"When the old man does right the poor boy after all, the poor boy gets no good of it.
He gets made away with, at the moment when he's lifting — as one may say — the cup and sarser to his lips."
"Cup and sarser" — Boffin's dialect rendering of cup and saucer — is pure Dickens.
It converts an abstraction — the cruelty of inheritance, the bitter irony of delayed justice — into something you can see and hold.
And that's the structural signature of this whole novel: the material world carrying the moral weight.
And what a voice Boffin has — Dickens gives him this marvellous combination of genuine warmth and phonetic eccentricity that is somehow never condescending.
As a performer, the moment that stops me cold in this passage is the description of old Harmon's violence — because it comes in the same register as everything else.
Listen to what Boffin actually says happened.

"I have seen him, after Mrs Boffin has given him her mind respecting the claims of the nat'ral affections, catch off Mrs Boffin's bonnet — she wore, in general, a black straw, perched as a matter of convenience on the top of her head — and send it spinning across the yard."
The parenthetical description of the bonnet — a black straw, perched on top of her head — is doing something extraordinary.
It interrupts the violence with a small, affectionate portrait of Mrs Boffin's cheerful practicality.
And then the sentence concludes — "and received flush on the temple.
Which dropped her, Mr Lightwood.
Dropped her."
Two words, repeated, and the repetition is the whole point — the weight of it, the blunt factual horror.
That's not rhetoric — that's a man who was there, who saw it, and cannot get past it.
Oliver's right that those two words land differently from everything around them — and I think it's because Boffin doesn't reach for a more dramatic phrase.
He doesn't say she fell, or she was hurt — he says she was dropped.
As if the force came from outside and simply eliminated her from the upright position.
What moves me about this whole passage is what it tells us about the Boffins' love for John Harmon — this child they couldn't protect, but kept trying to.
And that love doesn't disappear when he does — it becomes the engine for something remarkable.
And that's precisely where the novel does something that surprised me on re-reading — the grief doesn't freeze these characters, it propels them.
Caroline, you wanted to talk about what Mrs Boffin proposes to do with the inheritance.
Yes — because this is one of the quietly radical moments in the novel, and it can slip by if you're not paying attention.
Mrs Boffin has a fancy, as she calls it — almost apologetically.
And that fancy is this.
"Now that he is past all benefit of the money, and it's come to us, I should like to find some orphan child, and take the boy and adopt him and give him John's name, and provide for him."
She adds — and this breaks my heart slightly — "Somehow, it would make me easier, I fancy."
"Say it's only a whim" — as if she needs permission to be generous.
There's something of the Gothic about it too — keeping the name alive, as if memory itself could be a form of care.
What Caroline is pointing to structurally is that Dickens has set up a beautifully ironic doubling.
Mrs Boffin wants to find a surrogate John Harmon — and the real John Harmon is already in the house, hiding behind the name Rokesmith.
The identity she wants to preserve is the identity the man himself has deliberately surrendered.
It's a structural knot that Dickens draws tight very slowly, and the tenderness of Mrs Boffin's wish makes it all the more painful.
And Dickens is almost wickedly candid about this particular piece of plotting — which I find rather endearing.
He actually steps forward, authorial hat in hand, and tells us exactly what he was doing with the Harmon mystery.
There's a remarkable postscript in the novel where he addresses this directly.

"I foresaw the likelihood that a class of readers and commentators would suppose that I was at great pains to conceal exactly what I was at great pains to suggest: namely, that Mr John Harmon was not slain, and that Mr John Rokesmith was he."
There's a glorious archness to that.
He's not apologising — he's saying: you thought you were ahead of me, but I put the answer in plain sight.
And then — this is the bit I love — he asks for patience, "in the interests of art."
That authorial intervention is fascinating to me as a novelist — because it speaks to the serialised format, the weekly installments, readers writing in with their guesses.
Dickens is managing his audience's expectations in real time — like a conductor who keeps glancing at the audience to see if they're with him.
And the phrase "in the interests of art" carries real weight — it's his defence of ambiguity as a legitimate artistic tool, not a failure of clarity.
He trusted the architecture to hold, even when readers were tugging at the load-bearing walls.
Though there's also something a little defensive about it, isn't there?
The slightly pointed phrase — "a class of readers and commentators" — suggests he's responding to actual criticism, not imagined obtuseness.
But what I find touching is that he clearly cared — that the Harmon mystery mattered to him as a piece of craftsmanship.
And the unmasking, when it finally comes — we should talk about how that is staged.
Because it isn't tender — it's cold, almost brutal, directed at a man who thoroughly deserves it.
Oliver, you've performed this kind of confrontation scene many times — what do you make of Harmon's voice when he finally speaks as himself?
It's a tremendous theatrical release — months of disguise, months of passivity, and then suddenly Harmon grabs Wegg by the cravat and becomes a different man entirely.
And the first word out of his mouth is "scoundrel."
Not a question, not a revelation — an accusation.
He has been watching Wegg for a very long time, and he wants Wegg to know that.
The speech he makes is remarkable for its controlled cruelty — he tells Wegg precisely why the game was prolonged.
"I kept you under good observation from my first appearance here, and though Sloppy has long made it the chief occupation and delight of his life, to attend you like your shadow."
"Attend you like your shadow" — Sloppy, this great lumbering innocent, as Wegg's appointed nemesis.
There's real relish in that detail — Dickens enjoying the irony that the humblest character has been the most effective spy.
What strikes me about that confrontation speech is the phrase "deluded, to the last possible moment" — it's precise, almost legalistic.
Harmon has been living inside a deception himself — and now he weaponises deception against a man who was planning to steal from his benefactors.
There's a symmetry there that feels deeply satisfying — the novel's central engine of disguise finally turning in the right direction.
And the phrase about the "heaviest possible disappointment" — that's not justice, exactly.
That's revenge, carefully calibrated.
I keep coming back to how long John Harmon has held this secret — from the Boffins, from Bella, from everyone who cared about him.
And then remembering that Mrs Boffin wanted to find an orphan and name him John — when the real John was there all along, watching.
There's something both comic and quietly aching about that.
The novel holds comedy and grief in the same hand — and that, I think, is what we'll be returning to throughout this series.
We've been looking today at how the Harmon inheritance poisons and propels the story from its very first pages — and how Dickens himself insisted on our patience with his design.
In our next segment, we'll be moving to the river — and to the world of scavenging and salvage that runs beneath this story like an underground current.

segments.title: Bella's Reckoning: Greed, Affection, and Self-Discovery

utterances.text: Welcome to Our Mutual Friend Unpacked, the programme where we take Dickens's last completed novel apart scene by scene — and put it back together with fresh eyes.
I'm your host, and today we're deep inside one of the novel's most searching story lines: the moral education of Bella Wilfer.
Bella begins the novel as a self-confessed mercenary, determined to marry for money — and what follows is a slow, funny, sometimes excruciating reckoning with that ambition.
Joining me today are three guests who know this novel with real intimacy.

Dr Eleanor Hartley is a literary critic and novelist whose great gift is making the craft of fiction feel thrilling — she reads Dickens like a fellow practitioner, with enormous admiration and a little professional envy.
Oliver Trevelyan is an actor and writer who has given voice to more classic novels than almost anyone alive — he hears the prose as performance, and he'll bring that ear to every passage we discuss.

And Caroline Woodcourt is a book critic who has lived with Our Mutual Friend since her teens, returning to it again and again — her readings are intimate, emotionally precise, and fiercely opinionated.
Let's begin where Mr Boffin begins: with money.
What I find so architecturally brilliant about these Boffin scenes is that Dickens is running two stories simultaneously and neither one tips its hand too soon.
On the surface, Mr Boffin is corrupting — the Golden Dustman turned miser, turned advocate for naked greed.
But the deeper story is Bella being forced to see her own values reflected back at her — and finding the reflection unbearable.
That dark cloud description is where Dickens makes the gothic charge explicit.
"A dark cloud of suspicion, covetousness, and conceit, overshadowing the once open face."
Three abstract nouns in a single devastating phrase — and that word 'once' carrying all the grief of what's been lost.
Dickens doesn't describe the change in Boffin gradually — he gives it to us as a weather event, sudden and total.
And what a gift it is to perform, that weather-event quality.
But before we get to the darkness, I must have the charity speech, because it is one of the finest comic arias in the book.
Old Boffin working himself up into a magnificent rage about patronage titles — it has the rhythm of a man who has been wanting to say this for years.
Listen to the accumulation here:

"Patrons and Patronesses, and Vice-Patrons and Vice-Patronesses, and Deceased Patrons and Deceased Patronesses, and Ex-Vice-Patrons and Ex-Vice-Patronesses, what does it all mean in the books of the Charities that come pouring in on Rokesmith as he sits among 'em pretty well up to his neck!"
The list is the joke — each new category more absurd than the last — but then that image of Rokesmith drowning in the paperwork lands as a genuine punchline.
And Dickens has timed it perfectly: 'pretty well up to his neck' — the slang arriving just as the rhetoric has built to bursting.
What I keep coming back to is how uncomfortable those speeches make Bella — and by extension, how uncomfortable they make us.
Because Boffin isn't wrong, exactly.
The novel's world does reward the rich.
When he tells Bella to go in for money, he's giving her the most practical advice in the book.
"Go in for money, my love. Money's the article. You'll make money of your good looks, and of the money Mrs Boffin and me will have the pleasure of settling upon you, and you'll live and die rich."
That 'live and die rich' — there's something almost liturgical about it.
As though wealth were the proper end of human life, the blessed state.
And Dickens lets it hang there — unctuous, as the narrator says — for us to feel the wrongness of it.
That scene in Bella's room, with the looking-glass, is where Dickens does something I find genuinely dazzling.
He gives Bella an internal monologue that enacts the very contradiction it describes.
She interrogates herself, and the questioning becomes a kind of self-prosecution.
The passage is worth hearing in full:

"What he said was very sensible, I am sure, and very true, I am sure. It is only what I often say to myself. Don't I like it then? No, I don't like it, and, though he is my liberal benefactor, I disparage him for it."
And then — my favourite moment — she turns on herself directly:
"Then pray, what do you mean by this, you inconsistent little Beast?"
That 'Beast' — capitalised in spirit if not always on the page — is Dickens catching a real psychological moment: the sudden, almost violent self-contempt.
When I read that passage aloud, the looking-glass direction is everything.
Bella is both counsel and defendant — she splits herself in two and conducts the trial in a mirror.
It's pure theatre — and it connects directly to the later scene with Lizzie, where the self-poke becomes the physical version of the same reckoning.
Dickens sets up the comic moment beautifully:
"There, you little mercenary wretch! Do you hear that? Ain't you ashamed of your self?"
And then she gives herself 'a penitential poke in the side' — which is the funniest act of conscience in Victorian fiction.
The body enacting what the mind has already decided — she has judged herself and the sentence is corporal.
And it matters enormously that the catalyst there is Lizzie Hexam.
Lizzie represents everything Bella's mercenary creed cannot account for — a love that asks for nothing, that costs everything.
When Lizzie describes what Eugene's eyes mean to her, Dickens gives her some of the most quietly devastating language in the novel.
"I would not have the light of them taken out of my life, for anything my life can give me."
'Anything my life can give me' — that's an absolute surrender, and it's entirely unironic.
In a novel so saturated with irony, that directness hits like cold water.
And Bella, sitting there next to her, feels the contrast in her bones — hence the poke.
What strikes me structurally is that Dickens refuses to make Bella's transformation a clean conversion.
She doesn't see Lizzie and immediately become a different person.
She pokes herself — which is both funny and genuinely small.
The transformation is cumulative — these repeated small recognitions, each one leaving a mark.
That's why the looking-glass device is so right — she keeps coming back to her own reflection, each time seeing something slightly different.
And that gradualness is, I think, what makes Bella one of Dickens's most convincingly human characters — she earns her transformation by resisting it first.
We've seen Bella interrogate herself, be lectured by a changed Boffin, and sit beside Lizzie's selfless devotion — and the discomfort accumulates beautifully.
In our next segment, we'll turn to the machinery behind that transformation — John Rokesmith, his secret, and the question of what it costs to test the person you love.

segments.title: The Art of Dickensian Voice: Narration, Interruption, and Effect

utterances.text: Welcome to Our Mutual Friend Unpacked, the show that takes Dickens's last completed novel seriously — and with great pleasure.
I'm your host, and today we're deep inside one of the novel's most demanding pleasures: the narrator's own voice.
Not what Dickens shows us, but how he tells it — the interventions, the ironies, the sudden moral proclamations that erupt out of the prose.
To explore that, I have three extraordinary companions with me today.
Dr. Eleanor Hartley is a novelist and creative writing teacher who cares deeply about how sentences are built and what they can carry.
She'll be our guide to Dickens's narrative architecture today.
Oliver Trevelyan has voiced more classic novels for audio than almost anyone alive, and he hears the prose the way a musician hears a score.
When Dickens writes for the voice, Oliver will be the first to notice.
And Caroline Woodcourt is a book critic who has lived with this novel since she was a teenager — she brings the reader's intimate, accumulated experience of these pages.
Caroline will tell us what it feels like when the narrator breaks cover — and why we love it when he does.
Eleanor, let's begin with you — the narrator of this novel has a habit of stepping forward and speaking directly, almost polemically.
What is Dickens doing when he does that, and does it work?
It works thrillingly — though it shouldn't, by any modern theory of fiction.
Dickens keeps transgressing the boundary between story and argument, and each time he does it, he makes you feel the novel is alive and thinking in front of you.
There's a passage early in the novel where he reflects on the Boffins — these unlettered, rough-edged people — and what their goodness has survived.
He builds through a long, qualifying sentence about their weaknesses and vanities, and then suddenly the narration tightens into a single axiomatic blow.
Listen to this:
"For, Evil often stops short at itself and dies with the doer of it; but Good, never."
Eight words after the semicolon: but Good, never.
The brevity is the point — he's been patient, he's qualified everything, and then he drives a spike into the floor.
And when you read it aloud, that semicolon is a held breath.
Dickens is composing for a voice, always — the punctuation is a conductor's score.
That sentence is actually two gestures: the long, almost exhausted description of evil burning itself out, and then the single triumphant word.
Never.
In performance I always let that land in total silence.
An audience — readers or listeners — they feel that.
What strikes me is that it doesn't feel like an intrusion.
By the time Dickens makes that proclamation, the novel has earned it.
We've watched the Boffins absorb cruelty and go on being good — we've seen that moral straightness, as he calls it.
So when the narrator steps forward and names it as eternal law, it doesn't feel imposed.
It feels confirmed.
That's exactly the structural logic — the narrator banks trust through observation, then spends it on declaration.
And he does something even stranger with Eugene Wrayburn — where the narration doesn't proclaim, but mimics.
Eugene is explaining to Mortimer that he has no plan — that he lives entirely in the present moment and cannot contemplate consequences.
And Dickens lets Eugene's voice perform that very quality as he speaks:
"Fair means or foul means, are all alike to me. I ask you — for information — what does that mean?
When I have found her I may ask you — also for information — what do I mean now?"
He turns self-analysis into a game — and the parenthetical repetition of 'for information' is both comic and genuinely unsettling.
He doesn't know what he means — and the sentence enacts that not-knowing beautifully.
Every time I've performed Eugene, that speech nearly defeats me — in the best possible way.
Because the comedy and the dread are perfectly superimposed.
'Fair means or foul means' — said with that airy Eugene elegance — is actually a man announcing he has no moral compass when it comes to Lizzie.
And he's not even sure he knows it.
The character's voice becomes the narrator's irony — Dickens doesn't need to editorialize, because Eugene does it for him without realizing.
Whereas with Bradley Headstone, the narrator is anything but playful.
There's a passage where Dickens tracks Bradley's moral descent with almost surgical precision — measuring in fractions.
He writes:
"The baseness of confirming him in this suspicion or pretence of one (for he could not have really entertained it), was a line's breadth beyond the mark the schoolmaster had reached."
A line's breadth.
He's measuring Bradley's corruption the way you'd measure a fault line — not in leaps but in infinitesimal increments.
And the parenthetical — 'for he could not have really entertained it' — is the narrator quietly insisting that even Bradley knows he has crossed into something fabricated and vile.
That parenthetical is doing so much work — it's a moral bracket, isn't it?
Dickens can't just narrate Bradley's actions — he needs to adjudicate them in real time.
And notice the escalation: 'the baseness... was attained' — he's using the language of achievement, grotesquely.
Bradley has accomplished something — just something terrible.
And then: 'He made no reply, but walked on with a lowering face.' — the narrator steps back out, and the image is left to chill us.
Which brings me to Riderhood — because the narration shifts again when Dickens describes him pursuing Bradley.
There's a passage of pure, almost admiring description — no moralizing, no brackets.
Just this:
"He was a better follower than Bradley. It had been the calling of his life to slink and skulk and dog and waylay, and he knew his calling well."
That list — slink and skulk and dog and waylay — it's a catalogue of villainy rendered with a craftsman's relish.
Dickens cannot help admiring excellence, even in a scoundrel.
And that phrase — 'the doomed Bradley' — drops in like a black stone.
'The doomed Bradley' — the narrator knows the ending before we do, and he lets that knowledge show for just a moment.
That's the god-trick of the omniscient narrator — deployed rarely enough that when it comes, it lands like ice water.
And there's one more mode I want to mention — the narrator who becomes lyrical, almost delirious.
There's a passage where he gives us Rokesmith's secret longing for Bella, filtered through the noise of a train.
"O boofer lady, fascinating boofer lady! If I were but legally executor of Johnny's will!
If I had but the right to pay your legacy and to take your receipt!"
It's absurd — legal vocabulary doing the work of a love lyric — and completely, heartbreakingly right.
That passage is extraordinary precisely because the narrator steps fully inside a consciousness the character himself cannot acknowledge.
Rokesmith can't declare himself — the whole novel has gagged him with disguise.
So the narrator cries out for him, in this extravagant, slightly mad apostrophe.
And the train becomes a co-conspirator — 'all knowingly shutting up their green eyes and opening their red ones.'
The whole world is in on the secret that John Rokesmith cannot speak.
It's the narrator as co-sufferer — weeping on behalf of a character sworn to silence.
And only Dickens can go from that tenderness to 'slink and skulk and dog and waylay' in the same novel and have it feel unified rather than incoherent.
The narrator's voice is the spine that holds everything together — the comic, the tragic, the polemical, the lyrical.
The spine — I love that.
Evil that dies with the doer, a man who doesn't know what he means, baseness measured in line's breadths, and a train complicit in a love that cannot speak its name.
All of it held together by a narrator who is moralist, comedian, lyric poet, and cold-eyed judge — sometimes within a single paragraph.
We'll be back after a short break to look at how Dickens handles money — its language, its corruption, and what this novel dares to say about it.

segments.title: Dust, Money, and Moral Rot: Boffin's Ascent and Fall

utterances.text: Welcome back to Our Mutual Friend Unpacked.
Today we're going deep into one of the novel's great sustained satirical performances — the world of dust, money, and moral rot that surrounds Nicodemus Boffin.
Boffin inherits a fortune built on dust heaps, moves into an aristocratic mansion, and almost immediately becomes a target — for beggars, schemers, and worse.
To help us unpack all of this, I'm joined by three wonderful readers of Dickens.
Eleanor Hartley is a novelist and creative writing teacher whose eye for the architecture of fiction — the structural choices, the image that carries a chapter's weight — is simply unmatched.

Oliver Trevelyan has recorded more classic novels as audiobooks than perhaps anyone alive, and he comes to every text as a performer — hearing rhythms, catching comic timing, feeling exactly where Dickens wrote for the voice.

And Caroline Woodcourt is a book critic who first read this novel as a teenager and has returned to it many times — she brings the reader's eye, the reader's heart, and very strong opinions about which characters deserve better.
Let's begin with Boffin's arrival in his new world — and what Dickens makes of it immediately.
What strikes me first about the way Dickens positions Boffin in that mansion is the opening phrase — 'the minion of fortune and the worm of the hour.'
Dickens immediately signals that this is ironically framed — and then he does something technically beautiful.
He gives us this extraordinary simile, and I want to read it because it's just too good to paraphrase.
'Like an eminently aristocratic family cheese, it was much too large for his wants, and bred an infinite amount of parasites.'
A cheese. He compares the aristocratic mansion to a cheese.
And the word 'parasites' does double work — it's the mould on the cheese and it's every hanger-on who descends on Boffin the moment his money becomes known.
One image, and you've got the whole satirical programme of what follows.
That simile is a gift for any reader performing the text — it gets a laugh every single time, and then the laugh cools into something more uncomfortable.
Because 'parasites' lands hard.
And what's wonderful is that Dickens doesn't let you forget it — the very next passages deliver the parasites in full catalogued glory.
The Secretary — this wonderfully deadpan figure — is sorting through letters, and Dickens starts counting.
'Fifty-seven churches to be erected with half-crowns, forty-two parsonage houses to be repaired with shillings, seven-and-twenty organs to be built with halfpence.'
That accumulation — those precise, absurd numbers — is pure comic percussion.
Dickens is a jazz musician here — he knows exactly when to add another instrument.
And then comes the Duke of Linseed.
Which is one of the great comic names in the novel, let's be honest.
Dickens sets it up with that gorgeous physical description of the letter itself.
'Large fat private double letter, sealed with ducal coronet.'
Six words before the quote even begins, and you can see the thing — feel its self-importance — sitting on the Secretary's desk.
And then the kicker — the whole florid ducal letter is lithographed by the hundred, with Boffin's name filled in by someone else entirely.
Rank condescension dressed up as personal favour. It's devastating.
That detail about the lithograph is doing something structurally important, I think.
It collapses the distinction between aristocratic charity and aristocratic exploitation.
The Duke isn't even bothering to pretend the letter is personal — and Dickens wants us to feel how little Boffin matters to these people, except as a source of money.
And it pairs so perfectly with the individual beggars in the next passage — who are at pains to be extravagantly personal, almost comically intimate.
The comparison Dickens makes there is wonderful — he says their documents
'are, as to papers deserving the name, what minced veal is to a calf.'
The brutality of that image — and the comedy — land simultaneously.
'Minced veal to a calf' — I mean, that's a line that plays beautifully aloud because it sounds absurd and then it becomes genuinely shocking.
And then Dickens just keeps going — the taxonomy of beggars is one of his great comic catalogues.
The daughters of generals who are long accustomed to every luxury — except spelling. That parenthetical is a dart.
And the inspired beggars — the ones sitting in the dark with a fragment of candle when an angel whispers Boffin's name.
The comic energy there is extraordinary — but underneath it you feel the actual desperation Dickens is describing.
He never lets the satire fully evacuate the human misery. That's what makes it sting.
That's exactly it — the beggars on horseback who need just one final thing: a clock, a violin, an astronomical telescope.
The list is funny, but it's also a portrait of people who have convinced themselves they're one lucky break away from salvation.
Which is not so very different from the novel's larger argument about money — that everyone in this world is waiting for a windfall to solve everything.
Boffin got his. And look what arrives immediately afterward.
And it's not just beggars from outside who pose a threat to Boffin's world — there's a threat far closer to home.
Silas Wegg has been poring over documents of his own — and he believes he's found a will that could destroy the Boffins entirely.
The will scene is a masterclass in comic menace.
Wegg reads the document to Mr Venus with this extraordinary blend of faux legal gravity and pantomime triumph.
And the will itself — what it says about old Harmon — is devastating in its terseness.

'Inasmuch as he has never made friends, and has ever had a rebellious family, he, John Harmon, gives to Nicodemus Boffin the Little Mound, which is quite enough for him, and gives the whole rest and residue of his property to the Crown.'
'Quite enough for him.' The contempt in those four words is breathtaking.
Old Harmon, from beyond the grave, still ranking Boffin — still telling him exactly how much he's worth in the scheme of things.
And crucially, Wegg is delighted by this. His glee is the glee of a man who has finally got leverage.
Which brings us to that extraordinary passage where Dickens anatomises Wegg's compulsion to hover over Boffin's house.
It's one of those moments where the narration steps back and becomes almost philosophical.
'Power — unless it be the power of intellect or virtue — has ever the greatest attraction for the lowest natures.'
Dickens names what Wegg is, baldly, without flinching.
And then the image: Wegg's 'power to strip the roof off the inhabiting family like the roof of a house of cards.'
A house of cards inside an aristocratic mansion. Fragility inside pomp. That's the whole novel in miniature.
What haunts me about that passage is the word 'unconscious.'
The 'unconscious house-front.' The house doesn't know what's coming. The Boffins don't know what's coming.
And Wegg standing there in the dark, savouring his secret — it's genuinely chilling, even through the satire.
Because money in this novel makes people vulnerable — it doesn't protect them.
The Boffins arrived in that mansion and became targets. Wegg is just the most malevolent expression of a general truth.
Power, parasites, and a will that demotes a man from beyond the grave — Dickens has given us a great deal to sit with.
What's emerged from this conversation, I think, is how the dust heaps aren't just a backdrop — they're an argument.
That wealth, in this novel, breeds exactly the rot it pretends to cure.
Thank you to Eleanor, Oliver, and Caroline — and we'll be back shortly to follow where all of this leads.

segments.title: Laughter in the Shadows: Dickens's Comic Mastery

utterances.text: Welcome to Our Mutual Friend Unpacked, the programme where we take one of the great novels of the English language and open it up, chapter by chapter, passage by passage.
I'm your host, and today we're exploring something that sits at the very heart of Dickens's genius: his comedy.
Not the easy laugh, not the cheap gag — but the kind of comic writing that makes you stop, re-read, and wonder how a sentence can do that much work simultaneously.
Joining me today are three guests who know this territory intimately.
Dr. Eleanor Hartley is a novelist and creative writing teacher whose eye for fictional architecture is, frankly, remarkable — she sees structural choices the rest of us miss entirely.
Oliver Trevelyan has narrated more classic novels for audio than perhaps anyone alive, and brings the performer's ear — he hears what Dickens wrote for the voice.
And Caroline Woodcourt is a book critic who has lived with this novel since her teens and returns to it with the devotion of a true believer.
Oliver, let's begin with you — because the passages in front of us today are yours, and they are irresistible.
Thank you — and I have to say, whenever I encounter the Boffins' household, I feel that particular Dickensian joy that is almost impossible to explain to someone who hasn't felt it.
There's a room described early in the novel — the room at the Bower — and it is, to my mind, one of the great comic set-pieces in all of Dickens.
The narrator sums it up in a single devastating sentence — let me read it to you:
'It was the queerest of rooms, fitted and furnished more like a luxurious amateur tap-room than anything else within the ken of Silas Wegg.'
'Luxurious amateur tap-room' — three words that shouldn't work together, and yet they define the Boffins perfectly before we've spent five minutes with them.
Then Dickens itemises the room, and this is where the comedy gets architectural.
The books 'ranged flat, in a row, like a galvanic battery' — there is something almost aggressive about that image, as though knowledge is being deployed rather than read.
And then the carpet that stops short at Mrs Boffin's footstool, giving way to sand and sawdust — the novel's whole comic vision of class aspiration in a single flooring detail.
What strikes me about that room is how precisely Dickens engineers the comedy through spatial contrast.
The garish drawing-room furniture placed beside the working-class settles — he isn't just describing a room, he's mapping a social collision.
And then there's the glorious detail of the stuffed birds and waxen fruits under glass on one side, and a cold joint and a large pie on the other.
Hollow ornamentation versus genuine nourishment — it's a moral diagram drawn in domestic objects.
And the comedy is doing real ideological work: the Boffins come out ahead of every fashionable household in the novel, precisely because their sand and sawdust is honest.
What I keep returning to is the phrase 'seemed to stand on tiptoe to exchange glances with Mr Wegg' — the case-bottles.
Dickens animates the room's objects as if they have social ambitions of their own.
The bottles are flirting with Wegg — and Wegg, we suspect, is going to respond.
The whole room is a character — which is very Dickens, but here it's done with such lightness of touch that you almost don't notice how precise it is.
Can I move to an entirely different register of comedy — because one of the passages I've been given is a masterclass in physical farce.
There's a scene involving an orphan — a chubby orphan — and a doorway board.
The narrator sets it up with this magnificent sentence — and I defy anyone to hear this without smiling:
'Being an orphan of a chubby conformation, he then took to rolling, and had rolled into the gutter before they could come up.'
'An orphan of a chubby conformation' — the formal Latinate phrase applied to a tumbling baby is inspired.
And the word 'conformation' — it sounds like the orphan has been professionally assessed and found to be round.
Then the doorway board catches everyone — Mrs Higden coming out, Mrs Boffin and Rokesmith going in — and the orphan ends up upside down and purple in the countenance.
It's a scene written for performance — every beat timed, every absurdity earned.
There's something technically brilliant in that passage that I think is easy to miss on first reading.
The narrator says the cries of the orphan 'imparted a lugubrious and inhuman character' to the situation.
'Lugubrious and inhuman' — those are words you'd use for an industrial accident, not a tumbling baby.
Dickens is simultaneously making us laugh and reminding us that this child is an orphan — genuinely vulnerable, genuinely at risk of being in unlawful possession of nobody at all.
The comedy and the pathos are running in the same channel — which is a much harder technical achievement than keeping them separate.
I want to bring in Betty Higden here — because the same chapter gives us one of the most quietly perfect lines in the novel.
Betty is explaining Sloppy's gift for reading the newspaper aloud, and she says — and the simplicity of this just kills me:
'He do the Police in different voices.'
Six words — and in those six words you have Betty Higden's whole world: the newspaper as entertainment, Sloppy's remarkable gift, the way spoken performance compensates for limited literacy.
It's funny — Sloppy doing police reports in different voices is a glorious image — and it's also a portrait of deep tenderness between two people society has largely abandoned.
That line has had a rather distinguished afterlife, actually — but let's not go there.
What I find fascinating as a performer is that 'He do the Police in different voices' is itself a kind of stage direction.
Betty is telling us: this is what good reading sounds like — it differentiates, it inhabits, it performs.
Dickens himself was a famous reader of his own work, and he absolutely did the police in different voices.
Now — I have to bring up the school passage, because to my mind it's the most ferociously funny sustained piece of satire in the book.
The narrator describes a school that maintains 'a grimly ludicrous pretence that every pupil was childish and innocent.'
Young women old in the vices of hard life are expected to be enthralled by Little Margery from the village cottage — who divides her porridge with singing birds.
The savage comedy of that gap — between actual lived experience and the approved improving literature — is really the whole Victorian class system in miniature.
And then the prose itself goes wild — listen to this:
'An exceedingly and confoundingly perplexing jumble of a school, in fact, where black spirits and grey, red spirits and white, jumbled jumbled jumbled jumbled, jumbled every night.'
The repetition of 'jumbled' isn't incidental — it's Dickens enacting the chaos he's describing, turning the syntax itself into a kind of madness.
Reading that passage aloud is one of the great technical challenges in the novel, I can tell you.
Because there's the Sunday-school section where the 'chief executioner' holds forth and the volunteer boy goes around smoothing the faces of inattentive children.
Dickens calls it 'smoothing' — this brutal face-pressing administered to any child who shows signs of life.
And then — the narrator explains that the infants were exchanging measles, rashes, whooping-cough, fever, and stomach disorders, 'as if they were assembled in High Market for the purpose.'
'High Market for the purpose' — it's the most Dickensian possible way of saying: this institution is making children ill.
What moves me is that even in the most satirically ferocious passages, Dickens keeps the humanity of the children in sight.
'An inclined plane of unfortunate infants' — that phrase makes them both ridiculous and heartbreaking.
They are being processed, geometrically arranged, handed over — and yet they are infants, flushed and exhausted and catching each other's illnesses.
The anger driving the satire is inseparable from the tenderness that makes it hurt.
Before we leave this territory, I want to touch on a passage of an entirely different tone — the scene with Lizzie and Jenny Wren at the fire.
It's not primarily comic — it's tender, almost pastoral — and yet it has the same quality of verbal music as the funniest passages.
Lizzie unbraids Jenny's hair — and listen to how Dickens describes it:
'it fell in a beautiful shower over the poor shoulders that were much in need of such adorning rain.'
'Adorning rain' — it's a metaphor of such unexpected generosity.
And the 'poor shoulders' carries the whole weight of Jenny's physical suffering, slipped in quietly beneath the beauty of the image.
That scene is one I return to again and again — because it shows Dickens at his most intimate.
Jenny then loosens Lizzie's dark hair, and it falls 'in two rich masses' — and then there's this beautiful piece of staging where Jenny lays her cheek against the dark folds.
She is ostensibly comparing their hair colours, but what she's actually doing is hiding — hiding behind Lizzie, so that Lizzie's face is revealed in the firelight.
Jenny gives Lizzie the light, and takes the shadow for herself — and you don't need to be told what that means about this friendship.
What strikes me about that passage, structurally, is the management of perspective.
The narrator says Jenny 'so managed a mere touch or two of her nimble hands' — and that word 'managed' is doing enormous work.
It suggests strategy, deliberateness — Jenny is an artist of care, and she's orchestrating this scene with the same precision she brings to her dolls.
And it loops back to everything Oliver said about the Bower — Dickens uses spaces and objects and physical arrangements to carry meaning that would be clumsy if stated outright.
What I find so striking, listening to all three of you, is how often in this novel the comedy and the tenderness are not alternatives — they're the same instrument played at different registers.
The chubby orphan rolling into the gutter, the carpet that stops at Mrs Boffin's footstool, Jenny managing Lizzie's hair in the firelight — they're all doing the same thing.
They're using the particular and the physical to carry what can't be said directly.
We'll be back shortly to explore another dimension of this extraordinary novel — stay with us.

segments.title: Transformation and Truth: Reading the Final Revelations

utterances.text: Welcome back to Our Mutual Friend Unpacked.
We've arrived at one of the novel's great structural payoffs — the moment when disguise is stripped away and truth comes flooding in.
John Harmon's confession, Boffin's revelation, and the extraordinary business of the Dutch bottle.
Eleanor is going to take us inside the architecture of Harmon's self-revelation — the extraordinary passage where he reasons himself into existence, almost.
Oliver will bring us the confrontation with Wegg — which is, frankly, one of the most satisfying scenes in the whole novel.
And Caroline will hold the emotional thread — asking what all of this costs, and what it finally means for Bella and for Harmon himself.
Eleanor — let's begin with that strange, circling monologue where Harmon addresses himself in the second person.
That passage is one of the strangest and most technically daring things Dickens ever wrote.
Harmon doesn't simply confess — he conducts a cross-examination of himself, out loud, in front of Bella.
The structural pivot is that extraordinary moment: 'Now, stop, and so far think it out, John Harmon. Is that so? That is exactly so.'
He splits himself into interrogator and witness simultaneously — it's almost dissociative, and entirely deliberate.
But what makes it devastating is what he's confirming under that self-interrogation.
'I came back, shrinking from my father's money, shrinking from my father's memory, mistrustful of being forced on a mercenary wife.'
That triple repetition — shrinking, shrinking, mistrustful — is almost incantatory.
He's not explaining himself to Bella so much as he's building himself — sentence by sentence — back into coherent selfhood.
And the voice is so peculiar — so unlike anything else in the novel — because it's a voice performing sincerity.
Harmon has been disguised for so long that even his confession carries the cadence of a man who isn't quite sure he's allowed to tell the truth yet.
When I read that passage aloud in the studio, I always find myself slowing almost to a halt at 'knowing of nothing but wretchedness that my father's wealth had ever brought about.'
The sentence just — stops itself.
Which is exactly what Harmon does — he stops, holds the thought, and then verifies it.
It's a writer trusting the reader to feel the weight of a pause as much as a word.
What moves me most in that passage is the mention of his sister — almost parenthetical, almost unbearable.
'The two dear noble honest friends who had made the only sunlight in my childish life or that of my heartbroken sister.'
She's already dead by the time he speaks those words.
He carries her through the whole novel as a kind of silent wound.
And then, at the end, we learn the full horror — that the last will actively reviled both of them by name.
Which brings us to that will — and to the Dutch bottle — and to one of the most theatrical confrontations in all of Dickens.
Oliver, you've performed this scene more than once — what's the playing of it?
The Wegg confrontation is pure Dickensian theatre — and I mean that as the highest compliment.
Harmon has been patient, watchful, dignified through the whole middle stretch of the novel.
And then the moment comes, and what we get is — violence and delight in equal measure.
Here is the line that I think no audiobook narrator has ever read without genuine relish.
'I mean to knock your head against the wall — and I'd give a thousand pounds for leave to knock your brains out.'
'Suiting his action to his words, with the heartiest good will' — Dickens gives us that stage direction inside the narration.
He is actively, physically enjoying this — and we are meant to enjoy it with him.
It is catharsis dressed as comedy, and Dickens knows exactly what he's doing.
There's a structural brilliance to how Dickens times the will's revelation here — it's not enough to expose Wegg, he must be demolished.
The Dutch bottle document is already superseded by the will proved by Boffin — Wegg's weapon was always a ghost.
And Harmon announces it with this magnificent, almost contemptuous calm.
'It is a will of my late father's, of more recent date than the will proved by Mr Boffin — leaving the whole of his property to the Crown.'
And then, mid-sentence, comes that magnificent parenthetical threat: 'address whom again, as you have addressed him already, and I'll knock you down.'
The narration notes he delivers this 'with as much indifference as was compatible with extreme sternness' — which is Dickens's prose at its most precise.
But I keep coming back to the passage about the Dutch bottle and what it actually contains — because it's not just a legal document, is it.
It's the father's cruelty, preserved in glass, buried in a mound of refuse — there's a symbolism there that doesn't feel accidental.
When Harmon explains what that will actually said, the language is shattering.
'That will gives everything absolutely to my noble benefactor and yours, Mr Boffin, excluding and reviling me, and my sister — then already dead of a broken heart — by name.'
Dead of a broken heart, and still named in the will to be publicly scorned.
The father's malice outlived even his children.
And Boffin — good, generous Boffin — buried it so the slur would never see the light.
That is the moral heart of the whole Boffin plot, isn't it.
Everyone in the novel suspects Boffin of becoming corrupted by wealth — and all along he's been quietly protecting the reputations of two dead children.
And Harmon's accounting of it — 'his great generous motive' — lands so simply after all that baroque plotting.
The paper in Wegg's hand is described at the very end as worth 'less than the rotten cork of the Dutch bottle.'
All that scheming, all that prodding and poking through the dust heaps — for a rotten cork.
And it's worth noting how Dickens arranges the information — Harmon has known all of this for some time.
His speech to Wegg is not improvised revelation — it's controlled demolition.
'The first thing you saw him do, and the second thing has been done without your knowledge' — every step was prepared.
The novel rewards patience — both Harmon's and the reader's.
There's something almost musical about the way Dickens times all of this — the slow accumulation of secrets and then the sudden release.
Caroline, you mentioned earlier what this costs Harmon — the passage where he speaks of his father's world.
What does the novel ultimately say about whether he — and Bella — can escape that inheritance?
I think that's the deepest question the novel asks — and it doesn't answer it simply.
Harmon comes to England, in his own words, 'knowing of nothing but wretchedness that my father's wealth had ever brought about.'
And yet by the novel's end, he is that wealth's principal beneficiary — and apparently at peace with it.
Dickens gets away with it because Bella's transformation is so thoroughly dramatised — we believe she has changed, genuinely changed.
But Harmon's resolution feels earned in a different, quieter way — through the very act of naming his fear out loud.
There's that extraordinary quality to Harmon's self-interrogation — the 'Is that so? That is exactly so' — of someone who has never been allowed to simply be truthful before.
He's spent the whole novel as a performance — Rokesmith, the lodger, the secretary — and now he's checking whether the real self still exists.
The answer is yes — but only because Bella loved him without knowing who he was.
That's the proof that the identity beneath the disguise was worth something.
And what a relief, after all the grimness of the dust heaps and the river and the Veneerings, that it ends there — with love as the test of character, not money.
Though — and I say this with great affection — Dickens does also give Harmon the money in the end.
He is not above a comfortable resolution.
He is emphatically not above a comfortable resolution.
Thank you all — Eleanor, Oliver, Caroline — for unpacking a set of scenes that reward exactly this kind of close attention.
The Dutch bottle, the self-interrogation, the knock on the wall — Dickens, at full stretch.
We'll be back shortly with our next segment.

segments.title: Our Mutual Friend: Bonds, Corruption, and Redemption

utterances.text: We've spent this episode tracing the great moral architecture of Our Mutual Friend — the river, the dust, the money, the people caught in between.
Before we close, I want to give each of our guests the chance to leave us with what stays with them — the image, the line, the moment that won't let go.
Eleanor, you've been thinking throughout about thematic depth and the novel's moral architecture — where does it all land for you?
What stays with me is the novel's insistence that corruption and redemption aren't opposites — they're woven from the same thread.
Take the very opening. Gaffer Hexam pulls himself up out of the dark water with money in his hand.
And Dickens gives us this extraordinary ritual — almost liturgical in its deliberateness.
Listen to the prose:
"He chinked it once, and he blew upon it once, and he spat upon it once,—'for luck,' he hoarsely said—before he put it in his pocket."
Three actions, perfectly balanced, perfectly grotesque — and that single word, 'hoarsely,' carrying the full weight of a man who has made his peace with the dead.
The money comes out of the river and it is already dirty before Gaffer even touches it. That's Dickens's thesis in one image.
And then Wegg sits at the other end of the book and proves the thesis correct — by constructing his own grotesque liturgy around money he hasn't even touched yet.
The Wegg and Venus conspiracy is one of the great comic set-pieces in all of Dickens.
The sheer escalating grandiosity of Wegg's rhetoric — 'comrade, brother, and partner' repeated until it becomes incantation.
And then comes this wonderful, perfectly timed word — delivered like a conjuror producing the rabbit.
"He considered it plain that such price was stateable in a single expressive word, and that the word was, 'Halves!'"
And then — almost immediately — he hedges. Perhaps it should be two-thirds. Perhaps three-fourths. He remains 'ever open to correction.'
That is a man who has convinced himself that greed is merely a question of fair arithmetic.
What strikes me is how the novel refuses to let money have the last word — not in the end.
There's a moment with Jenny Wren — her vision of the children in white — that sits outside all of that corruption completely.
She says these children came to her when she was small, dressed in white with something shining on their borders.
And they asked her —
"'Who is this in pain! Who is this in pain!' When I told them who it was, they answered, 'Come and play with us!'"
I can never read that without stopping. That repetition — 'Who is this in pain' — it lands somewhere very deep.
Jenny lives at the very bottom of the novel's social world — beaten, in pain, burdened — and Dickens gives her this private paradise of transcendence.
That is the counterweight to Gaffer and to Wegg. That is where the novel's heart is.
And then Bella — who begins the novel almost entirely defined by her hunger for wealth — chooses the other way entirely.
Her father's blessing of that choice is one of those Dickens speeches that walks a very fine comic and emotional line.
He keeps calling her 'this mercenary young person distantly related to myself' — it's the joke and the tenderness at once.
The actual declaration is this:
"My blessing on this engagement betwixt you, and she brings you a good fortune when she brings you the poverty she has accepted for your sake and the honest truth's!"
'The poverty she has accepted for your sake.' That is Dickens's moral counter-proposition to everything Gaffer does in that opening scene.
The same currency — poverty and money — but the meaning entirely reversed.
What I love is that Dickens doesn't sentimentalise it. The Cherub — Wilfer — is still making the speech a little too long, still pleased with himself.
Bella's hand is 'gradually stealing up his waistcoat to his neck' while he's orating. That's the warmth — the human comedy — that saves the scene from pure sermon.
Dickens always earns the emotion by keeping the comedy alive right up to the last moment.
And that's why, as a performer, I will never tire of this book. It gives you everything.
The river, the dust, the money, the pain, the play — and through it all, these extraordinary human beings Dickens refused to abandon.
My thanks to Eleanor Hartley, Oliver Trevelyan, and Caroline Woodcourt for a conversation that has done full justice to one of the great novels in the language.
Our Mutual Friend: still speaking, still alive, still asking — who is this in pain?

c8:p39.text:
‘And speaking of satisfactory,’ pursued Mr Boffin, ‘why, Lord save us!
      when we come to take it to pieces, bit by bit, where’s the
      satisfactoriness of the money as yet? When the old man does right the poor
      boy after all, the poor boy gets no good of it. He gets made away with, at
      the moment when he’s lifting (as one may say) the cup and sarser to his
      lips. Mr Lightwood, I will now name to you, that on behalf of the poor
      dear boy, me and Mrs Boffin have stood out against the old man times out
      of number, till he has called us every name he could lay his tongue to. I
      have seen him, after Mrs Boffin has given him her mind respecting the
      claims of the nat’ral affections, catch off Mrs Boffin’s bonnet (she wore,
      in general, a black straw, perched as a matter of convenience on the top
      of her head), and send it spinning across the yard. I have indeed. And
      once, when he did this in a manner that amounted to personal, I should
      have given him a rattler for himself, if Mrs Boffin hadn’t thrown herself
      betwixt us, and received flush on the temple. Which dropped her, Mr
      Lightwood. Dropped her.’
c8:p39.summary: Boffin details how he and Mrs Boffin repeatedly defended young John Harmon against Old Harmon's cruelty, including an incident where Harmon struck Mrs Boffin and she collapsed, establishing their selfless advocacy for the boy.
c8:p39.best_quote: I have seen him, after Mrs Boffin has given him her mind respecting the claims of the nat'ral affections, catch off Mrs Boffin's bonnet (she wore, in general, a black straw, perched as a matter of convenience on the top of her head), and send it spinning across the yard... and received flush on the temple. Which dropped her, Mr Lightwood. Dropped her.

c9:p23.text:
Mrs Boffin pulled his nearest ear, in acknowledgment of this piece of
      philosophy, and then said, gradually toning down to a motherly strain:
      ‘Last, and not least, I have taken a fancy. You remember dear little John
      Harmon, before he went to school? Over yonder across the yard, at our
      fire? Now that he is past all benefit of the money, and it’s come to us, I
      should like to find some orphan child, and take the boy and adopt him and
      give him John’s name, and provide for him. Somehow, it would make me
      easier, I fancy. Say it’s only a whim—’
c9:p23.summary: Mrs Boffin proposes adopting an orphan child, naming him John Harmon in memory of the young heir who drowned, thereby using their inherited fortune for redemptive good.
c9:p23.best_quote: Now that he is past all benefit of the money, and it's come to us, I should like to find some orphan child, and take the boy and adopt him and give him John's name, and provide for him.

c67:p57.text:
When I devised this story, I foresaw the likelihood that a class of
      readers and commentators would suppose that I was at great pains to
      conceal exactly what I was at great pains to suggest: namely, that Mr John
      Harmon was not slain, and that Mr John Rokesmith was he. Pleasing myself
      with the idea that the supposition might in part arise out of some
      ingenuity in the story, and thinking it worth while, in the interests of
      art, to hint to an audience that an artist (of whatever denomination) may
      perhaps be trusted to know what he is about in his vocation, if they will
      concede him a little patience, I was not alarmed by the anticipation.
c67:p57.summary: Dickens explains that he intentionally created ambiguity about John Harmon's identity and asks readers to trust his artistic judgment and patience with the serialized format.
c67:p57.best_quote: I foresaw the likelihood that a class of readers and commentators would suppose that I was at great pains to conceal exactly what I was at great pains to suggest: namely, that Mr John Harmon was not slain, and that Mr John Rokesmith was he.

c64:p99.text:
‘Now, scoundrel,’ said John Harmon, taking another sailor-like turn on his
      cravat and holding him in his corner at arms’ length, ‘I shall make two
      more short speeches to you, because I hope they will torment you. Your
      discovery was a genuine discovery (such as it was), for nobody had thought
      of looking into that place. Neither did we know you had made it, until
      Venus spoke to Mr Boffin, though I kept you under good observation from my
      first appearance here, and though Sloppy has long made it the chief
      occupation and delight of his life, to attend you like your shadow. I tell
      you this, that you may know we knew enough of you to persuade Mr Boffin to
      let us lead you on, deluded, to the last possible moment, in order that
      your disappointment might be the heaviest possible disappointment. That’s
      the first short speech, do you understand?’
c64:p99.summary: Harmon explains that they discovered Wegg's find through Venus, watched him closely, and deliberately prolonged his deception to maximize his disappointment.
c64:p99.best_quote: I kept you under good observation from my first appearance here, and though Sloppy has long made it the chief occupation and delight of his life, to attend you like your shadow.

c38:p42.text:
Bella ventured for a moment to look stealthily towards him under her
      eyelashes, and she saw a dark cloud of suspicion, covetousness, and
      conceit, overshadowing the once open face.
c38:p42.summary: Bella observes a dark expression of suspicion, covetousness, and conceit shadowing Mr Boffin's formerly open countenance.
c38:p42.best_quote: A dark cloud of suspicion, covetousness, and conceit, overshadowing the once open face.

c38:p55.text:
Somehow, Bella was not so well pleased with this assurance and this
      prospect as she might have been. Somehow, when she put her arms round Mrs
      Boffin’s neck and said Good Night, she derived a sense of unworthiness
      from the still anxious face of that good woman and her obvious wish to
      excuse her husband. ‘Why, what need to excuse him?’ thought Bella, sitting
      down in her own room. ‘What he said was very sensible, I am sure, and very
      true, I am sure. It is only what I often say to myself. Don’t I like it
      then? No, I don’t like it, and, though he is my liberal benefactor, I
      disparage him for it. Then pray,’ said Bella, sternly putting the question
      to herself in the looking-glass as usual, ‘what do you mean by this, you
      inconsistent little Beast?’
c38:p55.summary: Alone in her room, Bella grapples with her confused reaction to Mr Boffin's advice: she finds his sentiments sensible and true to her own desires, yet she is repelled by them and finds herself disparaging him for expressing them, finally questioning herself severely in the mirror.
c38:p55.best_quote: Why, what need to excuse him? What he said was very sensible, I am sure, and very true, I am sure. It is only what I often say to myself. Don't I like it then? No, I don't like it, and, though he is my liberal benefactor, I disparage him for it. Then pray, what do you mean by this, you inconsistent little Beast?

c31:p109.text:
‘I don’t. And if  they  do, my dear, they ought to learn better,’ said Mr
      Boffin. ‘Patrons and Patronesses, and Vice-Patrons and Vice-Patronesses,
      and Deceased Patrons and Deceased Patronesses, and Ex-Vice-Patrons and
      Ex-Vice-Patronesses, what does it all mean in the books of the Charities
      that come pouring in on Rokesmith as he sits among ’em pretty well up to
      his neck! If Mr Tom Noakes gives his five shillings ain’t he a Patron, and
      if Mrs Jack Styles gives her five shillings ain’t she a Patroness? What
      the deuce is it all about? If it ain’t stark staring impudence, what do
      you call it?’
c31:p109.summary: Mr Boffin delivers a scathing critique of the proliferation of patronage titles and the pretension of charity donors who expect public recognition for their contributions.
c31:p109.best_quote: Patrons and Patronesses, and Vice-Patrons and Vice-Patronesses, and Deceased Patrons and Deceased Patronesses, and Ex-Vice-Patrons and Ex-Vice-Patronesses, what does it all mean in the books of the Charities that come pouring in on Rokesmith as he sits among 'em pretty well up to his neck!

c38:p47.text:
‘Not a bit, my dear,’ said Mr Boffin. ‘But I think it’s very creditable in
      you, at your age, to be so well up with the pace of the world, and to know
      what to go in for. You are right. Go in for money, my love. Money’s the
      article. You’ll make money of your good looks, and of the money Mrs Boffin
      and me will have the pleasure of settling upon you, and you’ll live and
      die rich. That’s the state to live and die in!’ said Mr Boffin, in an
      unctuous manner. ‘R—r—rich!’
c38:p47.summary: Mr Boffin emphatically advises Bella to pursue money above all else, declaring that she should capitalize on her beauty and the wealth they will bestow on her to become and remain rich.
c38:p47.best_quote: Go in for money, my love. Money's the article. You'll make money of your good looks, and of the money Mrs Boffin and me will have the pleasure of settling upon you, and you'll live and die rich.

c42:p156.text:
The question was so directly at variance with Bella’s views in life, as
      set forth to her father, that she said internally, ‘There, you little
      mercenary wretch! Do you hear that? Ain’t you ashamed of your self?’ and
      unclasped the girdle of her arms, expressly to give herself a penitential
      poke in the side.
c42:p156.summary: Bella experiences an internal moment of shame at her own mercenary values when confronted by Lizzie's selfless love, and literally punishes herself with a poke in the side.
c42:p156.best_quote: There, you little mercenary wretch! Do you hear that? Ain't you ashamed of your self?

c42:p162.text:
‘It was late upon a wretched night,’ said Lizzie, ‘when his eyes first
      looked at me in my old river-side home, very different from this. His eyes
      may never look at me again. I would rather that they never did; I hope
      that they never may. But I would not have the light of them taken out of
      my life, for anything my life can give me. I have told you everything now,
      my dear. If it comes a little strange to me to have parted with it, I am
      not sorry. I had no thought of ever parting with a single word of it, a
      moment before you came in; but you came in, and my mind changed.’
c42:p162.summary: Lizzie recalls the rainy night she first met Eugene and confesses that sharing her feelings with Bella has been healing, though unexpected.
c42:p162.best_quote: I would not have the light of them taken out of my life, for anything my life can give me.

c9:p29.text:
These two ignorant and unpolished people had guided themselves so far on
      in their journey of life, by a religious sense of duty and desire to do
      right. Ten thousand weaknesses and absurdities might have been detected in
      the breasts of both; ten thousand vanities additional, possibly, in the
      breast of the woman. But the hard wrathful and sordid nature that had
      wrung as much work out of them as could be got in their best days, for as
      little money as could be paid to hurry on their worst, had never been so
      warped but that it knew their moral straightness and respected it. In its
      own despite, in a constant conflict with itself and them, it had done so.
      And this is the eternal law. For, Evil often stops short at itself and
      dies with the doer of it; but Good, never.
c9:p29.summary: Dickens reflects that the Boffins, though ignorant and unpolished, have been guided by genuine religious duty and moral righteousness that even hardened souls cannot entirely resist.
c9:p29.best_quote: For, Evil often stops short at itself and dies with the doer of it; but Good, never.

c43:p61.text:
‘Ah! See now! That’s exactly what I am incapable of doing. How very acute
      you are, Mortimer, in finding my weak place! When we were at school
      together, I got up my lessons at the last moment, day by day and bit by
      bit; now we are out in life together, I get up my lessons in the same way.
      In the present task I have not got beyond this:—I am bent on finding
      Lizzie, and I mean to find her, and I will take any means of finding her
      that offer themselves. Fair means or foul means, are all alike to me. I
      ask you—for information—what does that mean? When I have found
      her I may ask you—also for information—what do I mean now? But
      it would be premature in this stage, and it’s not the character of my
      mind.’
c43:p61.summary: Eugene explains his lifelong pattern of living day-to-day without foresight, and applies this to his current quest: he is focused on finding Lizzie by any means, but cannot yet contemplate what finding her will mean.
c43:p61.best_quote: Fair means or foul means, are all alike to me...When I have found her I may ask you—also for information—what do I mean now?

c44:p90.text:
The baseness of confirming him in this suspicion or pretence of one (for
      he could not have really entertained it), was a line’s breadth beyond the
      mark the schoolmaster had reached. The baseness of communing and
      intriguing with the fellow who would have set that stain upon her, and
      upon her brother too, was attained. The line’s breadth further, lay
      beyond. He made no reply, but walked on with a lowering face.
c44:p90.summary: The narrator explicitly marks Bradley's moral crossing: he achieves baseness by intriguing with Riderhood over a suspicion that would stain Lizzie's honor, falling just short of the final, worst baseness he has yet to commit.
c44:p90.best_quote: The baseness of confirming him in this suspicion or pretence of one (for he could not have really entertained it), was a line's breadth beyond the mark the schoolmaster had reached.

c57:p44.text:
He was a better follower than Bradley. It had been the calling of his life
      to slink and skulk and dog and waylay, and he knew his calling well. He
      effected such a forced march on leaving the Lock House that he was close
      up with him—that is to say, as close up with him as he deemed it
      convenient to be—before another Lock was passed. His man looked back
      pretty often as he went, but got no hint of him.  He  knew how to take
      advantage of the ground, and where to put the hedge between them, and
      where the wall, and when to duck, and when to drop, and had a thousand
      arts beyond the doomed Bradley’s slow conception.
c57:p44.summary: The narrator describes Riderhood's superior skills at pursuit, having spent his life learning to follow, hide, and waylay victims.
c57:p44.best_quote: He was a better follower than Bradley. It had been the calling of his life to slink and skulk and dog and waylay, and he knew his calling well.

c42:p204.text:
O boofer lady, fascinating boofer lady! If I were but legally executor of
      Johnny’s will! If I had but the right to pay your legacy and to take your
      receipt!—Something to this purpose surely mingled with the blast of
      the train as it cleared the stations, all knowingly shutting up their
      green eyes and opening their red ones when they prepared to let the boofer
      lady pass.
c42:p204.summary: In the chapter's final lines, the narrator reveals Rokesmith's secret longing—that he were John Harmon so he could claim Bella as his wife and fulfill the inheritance's promise.
c42:p204.best_quote: If I were but legally executor of Johnny's will! If I had but the right to pay your legacy and to take your receipt!

c25:p0.text:
The minion of fortune and the worm of the hour, or in less cutting
      language, Nicodemus Boffin, Esquire, the Golden Dustman, had become as
      much at home in his eminently aristocratic family mansion as he was likely
      ever to be. He could not but feel that, like an eminently aristocratic
      family cheese, it was much too large for his wants, and bred an infinite
      amount of parasites; but he was content to regard this drawback on his
      property as a sort of perpetual Legacy Duty. He felt the more resigned to
      it, forasmuch as Mrs Boffin enjoyed herself completely, and Miss Bella was
      delighted.
c25:p0.summary: Nicodemus Boffin, the newly wealthy Golden Dustman, has settled into his grand mansion, finding it oversized but content because Mrs Boffin and Bella are delighted.
c25:p0.best_quote: like an eminently aristocratic family cheese, it was much too large for his wants, and bred an infinite amount of parasites

c17:p4.text:
But no one knows so well as the Secretary, who opens and reads the
      letters, what a set is made at the man marked by a stroke of notoriety. Oh
      the varieties of dust for ocular use, offered in exchange for the gold
      dust of the Golden Dustman! Fifty-seven churches to be erected with
      half-crowns, forty-two parsonage houses to be repaired with shillings,
      seven-and-twenty organs to be built with halfpence, twelve hundred
      children to be brought up on postage stamps. Not that a half-crown,
      shilling, halfpenny, or postage stamp, would be particularly acceptable
      from Mr Boffin, but that it is so obvious he is the man to make up the
      deficiency. And then the charities, my Christian brother! And mostly in
      difficulties, yet mostly lavish, too, in the expensive articles of print
      and paper. Large fat private double letter, sealed with ducal coronet.
      ‘Nicodemus Boffin, Esquire. My Dear Sir,—Having consented to preside
      at the forthcoming Annual Dinner of the Family Party Fund, and feeling
      deeply impressed with the immense usefulness of that noble Institution and
      the great importance of its being supported by a List of Stewards that
      shall prove to the public the interest taken in it by popular and
      distinguished men, I have undertaken to ask you to become a Steward on
      that occasion. Soliciting your favourable reply before the 14th instant, I
      am, My Dear Sir, Your faithful Servant,  Linseed . P.S. The Steward’s fee is
      limited to three Guineas.’ Friendly this, on the part of the Duke of
      Linseed (and thoughtful in the postscript), only lithographed by the
      hundred and presenting but a pale individuality of an address to Nicodemus
      Boffin, Esquire, in quite another hand. It takes two noble Earls and a
      Viscount, combined, to inform Nicodemus Boffin, Esquire, in an equally
      flattering manner, that an estimable lady in the West of England has
      offered to present a purse containing twenty pounds, to the Society for
      Granting Annuities to Unassuming Members of the Middle Classes, if twenty
      individuals will previously present purses of one hundred pounds each. And
      those benevolent noblemen very kindly point out that if Nicodemus Boffin,
      Esquire, should wish to present two or more purses, it will not be
      inconsistent with the design of the estimable lady in the West of England,
      provided each purse be coupled with the name of some member of his
      honoured and respected family.
c17:p4.summary: The Secretary describes the flood of charitable solicitations and scheme proposals that inundate the Boffins, including a satirical example of a duke's letter requesting Boffin become a Steward of a charity for a three-guinea fee.
c17:p4.best_quote: Large fat private double letter, sealed with ducal coronet.

c17:p5.text:
These are the corporate beggars. But there are, besides, the individual
      beggars; and how does the heart of the Secretary fail him when he has to
      cope with  them!  And they must be coped with to some extent, because they
      all enclose documents (they call their scraps documents; but they are, as
      to papers deserving the name, what minced veal is to a calf), the
      non-return of which would be their ruin. That is to say, they are utterly
      ruined now, but they would be more utterly ruined then. Among these
      correspondents are several daughters of general officers, long accustomed
      to every luxury of life (except spelling), who little thought, when their
      gallant fathers waged war in the Peninsula, that they would ever have to
      appeal to those whom Providence, in its inscrutable wisdom, has blessed
      with untold gold, and from among whom they select the name of Nicodemus
      Boffin, Esquire, for a maiden effort in this wise, understanding that he
      has such a heart as never was. The Secretary learns, too, that confidence
      between man and wife would seem to obtain but rarely when virtue is in
      distress, so numerous are the wives who take up their pens to ask Mr
      Boffin for money without the knowledge of their devoted husbands, who
      would never permit it; while, on the other hand, so numerous are the
      husbands who take up their pens to ask Mr Boffin for money without the
      knowledge of their devoted wives, who would instantly go out of their
      senses if they had the least suspicion of the circumstance. There are the
      inspired beggars, too. These were sitting, only yesterday evening, musing
      over a fragment of candle which must soon go out and leave them in the
      dark for the rest of their nights, when surely some Angel whispered the
      name of Nicodemus Boffin, Esquire, to their souls, imparting rays of hope,
      nay confidence, to which they had long been strangers! Akin to these are
      the suggestively-befriended beggars. They were partaking of a cold potato
      and water by the flickering and gloomy light of a lucifer-match, in their
      lodgings (rent considerably in arrear, and heartless landlady threatening
      expulsion ‘like a dog’ into the streets), when a gifted friend happening
      to look in, said, ‘Write immediately to Nicodemus Boffin, Esquire,’ and
      would take no denial. There are the nobly independent beggars too. These,
      in the days of their abundance, ever regarded gold as dross, and have not
      yet got over that only impediment in the way of their amassing wealth, but
      they want no dross from Nicodemus Boffin, Esquire; No, Mr Boffin; the
      world may term it pride, paltry pride if you will, but they wouldn’t take
      it if you offered it; a loan, sir—for fourteen weeks to the day,
      interest calculated at the rate of five per cent per annum, to be bestowed
      upon any charitable institution you may name—is all they want of
      you, and if you have the meanness to refuse it, count on being despised by
      these great spirits. There are the beggars of punctual business-habits
      too. These will make an end of themselves at a quarter to one P.M. on
      Tuesday, if no Post-office order is in the interim received from Nicodemus
      Boffin, Esquire; arriving after a quarter to one P.M. on Tuesday, it need
      not be sent, as they will then (having made an exact memorandum of the
      heartless circumstances) be ‘cold in death.’ There are the beggars on
      horseback too, in another sense from the sense of the proverb. These are
      mounted and ready to start on the highway to affluence. The goal is before
      them, the road is in the best condition, their spurs are on, the steed is
      willing, but, at the last moment, for want of some special thing—a
      clock, a violin, an astronomical telescope, an electrifying machine—they
      must dismount for ever, unless they receive its equivalent in money from
      Nicodemus Boffin, Esquire. Less given to detail are the beggars who make
